title: Developer tools — the questions before anything is drawn

steps.headline: These are two separate tools. Which should be designed and built first?
steps.today: Neither exists. The app has a Development page in Settings with bug reporting, Known issues and Roadmap, and nothing that shows what a session is really doing or how the app is performing.
steps.problem: Each tool is a full feature on its own. Designing both at once doubles the number of decisions in every review and delays having either one to use.
steps.proposal: Build one, use it for a while, then build the other. Both stay planned either way.

options.label: X-ray view first
pros: It answers the question you hit most often: why is the model looping or acting strangely?
It reads files the app already saves, so it is the safer of the two to build.
Once built, it is also the best place to show the monitor's findings later.
cons: Freezes and slowdowns stay as hard to track down as they are today until the monitor follows.

options.label: Live monitor first
pros: Freezes and slowdowns get easier to catch sooner.
cons: It touches how the running app reports on itself, so it needs a change to the safety rule (asked below) before it can be built.
A strange-model problem still means reading raw files by hand until X-ray follows.

options.label: Both together
pros: Both arrive at the same time.
cons: Every review deck covers twice as much.
Neither is usable until both are finished.

steps.headline: Should these go through the full review route, or the short one?
steps.today: Big features go through the full route: these questions, picture decks, an outside tester trying the design, a written checklist of what counts as done that you sign, a stranger grading the result, then your final yes. Small, clear changes skip straight to one picture deck.
steps.problem: The full route asks more of your time and runs about a dozen helper sessions. The short route is faster but has nobody checking the work except me.
steps.proposal: Pick the route for both tools.

options.label: Full route
pros: These are new screens with many choices, which is exactly what the full route is for.
An outside tester and a grader catch things I would miss in my own work.
cons: More decks for you to answer: roughly four or five per tool.
Takes longer to arrive.

options.label: Short route
pros: Faster. You see one picture deck, then the finished thing.
cons: Fewer chances to change direction before it is built.
Nobody but me checks the result before you do.

steps.intro: A second way to view a session that shows every line of the conversation, in exact order, including everything the normal chat hides.

steps.headline: Is this the right list of things X-ray should show that normal chat hides?
steps.today: Normal chat throws away a lot before you see it: hidden reminders the app and Claude Code slip to the model, hook messages, skill and instruction files loaded into the conversation, the model's thinking, the summary written when a long chat is shortened, repeated text, interruption notices, and the exact inputs and full outputs of tool calls.
steps.problem: When the model loops or acts oddly, the cause is usually in exactly those hidden parts — a reminder it keeps reacting to, a tool that returned something unexpected — and today you can't see them without opening raw files.
steps.proposal: X-ray shows all of those, each one labelled with what kind of line it is. Yes means this list is right; No or Other means tell me what is missing or should stay hidden.

steps.headline: Should X-ray show the session file exactly as saved, or what the app understood from it?
steps.today: Every session is saved as a file on your computer, one line per event. The app reads that file, turns lines into chat bubbles, and drops or merges some along the way.
steps.problem: If X-ray shows only what the app understood, a bug in the app's reading looks identical to a model misbehaving, and you can't tell which one is at fault.
steps.proposal: Three ways to fill the X-ray view.

options.label: Saved file, marked
options.summary: Every saved line exactly as written, each tagged with what normal chat did with it: shown, hidden, or merged into another bubble.
pros: Shows the true record and whether the app handled it right, side by side.
Lets you tell an app bug from a model problem at a glance.
cons: Busier screen: every line carries a small tag.
Most work of the three.

options.label: Saved file only
pros: The exact truth, nothing interpreted.
Simpler to build.
cons: Can't tell you when the app itself dropped or mangled something.

options.label: What the app understood
pros: Closest to the normal chat, so least to get used to.
cons: Hides app bugs, which is half of what you want this for.
Some hidden lines are thrown away before this point, so they could never appear.

steps.path: Settings → Development, and the session's top bar
steps.headline: How should X-ray be switched on?
steps.today: There is no switch. Settings → Development has four rows, none of which change how chat looks.
steps.problem: Most people using the app should never stumble into X-ray, but when you need it you want it one press away, on the session that is misbehaving.

options.label: Unlock once, button per session
options.summary: A 'Developer tools' switch in Settings → Development. Once on, an X-ray button appears in each session's top bar and flips just that session between X-ray and normal chat.
pros: Invisible to anyone who hasn't turned developer tools on.
One press to flip the session you're looking at, and back.
Other open sessions stay in normal chat.
cons: One more button in the top bar while developer tools are on.

options.label: One switch for everything
options.summary: A single switch in Settings → Development turns every session into X-ray until you turn it off.
pros: Nothing new in the top bar.
cons: Three clicks into Settings every time you want to flip.
Every session changes, not just the one you're inspecting.

options.label: Keyboard shortcut only
pros: Nothing on screen at all.
cons: Easy to forget, and impossible on the phone.
Easy to trigger by accident with no clue what happened.

steps.headline: Which helpers should be built into the X-ray view?
steps.today: Nothing like this exists, so there are no helpers yet.
steps.problem: A plain list of every line is long. In a looping session it can be thousands of lines, and spotting the repeat by eye is slow.
steps.proposal: Pick every helper you want in the first version. Fewer means it arrives sooner; any left out can be added later.

options.label: Repeat finder
options.summary: Flags when the model makes the same tool call, or near-same, several times in a row, and jumps between them.
pros: Points straight at a loop instead of you scrolling for it.
cons: Can flag normal repetition, like re-reading a file after editing it.

options.label: Time and gaps
options.summary: Each line's time, and a marker where nothing happened for a long stretch.
pros: Shows where a session stalled or a tool hung.
cons: More numbers on every line.

options.label: Size of each line
options.summary: How big each message, tool input and tool output is, so you can see what is eating the model's memory.
pros: Explains sudden shortening of long chats, and slow or costly turns.
cons: Only an estimate for Claude Code sessions; exact for the app's own sessions.

options.label: Filter and search
options.summary: Show only some kinds of line (say, only tool calls and their results) and search within them.
pros: Cuts a thousand-line session down to what matters.
cons: One more row of controls at the top.

options.label: Copy any line
options.summary: Copy one line, or a selected stretch, exactly as saved — to paste into a bug report or a fixing session.
pros: Hands a fixing session the exact evidence instead of a description.
cons: Copied text can include private content from the session.

options.label: Call ↔ result jump
options.summary: Click a tool call to jump to its result, and back.
pros: Results can land far below their call; this saves hunting.
cons: Small, but one more thing to learn.

steps.headline: While a session is in X-ray, should you still be able to type and send messages?
steps.today: Normal chat has the message box at the bottom and updates live as the model works.
steps.problem: If X-ray is look-only, you have to flip back to normal chat every time you want to answer or stop the model — and a looping model is exactly when you want to stop it fast.
steps.proposal: X-ray updates live as the session runs, and keeps the normal message box and Stop button. Yes builds it that way; No makes X-ray look-only.

steps.headline: Should X-ray work on the desktop app only at first, or everywhere at once?
steps.today: The desktop app, the Android app and the remote web page share the same chat screen.
steps.problem: Because the screen is shared, X-ray will mostly come along for free — but the part that reads the saved session file is separate on each, and doubles the work and testing.
steps.proposal: Two ways to roll it out.

options.label: Desktop first
pros: Arrives sooner.
Desktop is where you do this kind of inspecting.
cons: The X-ray button is hidden on the phone and remote web until a follow-up.

options.label: Everywhere at once
pros: Works the same wherever you are.
cons: Roughly twice the work, and the Android half can't always be tested on this computer.

steps.intro: A way for a fixing session to see what your real app is doing — freezes, errors, slowdowns — while you use it.

steps.path: The rule every development session follows
steps.headline: Should development sessions be allowed to watch your real, running app if you switch that on?
steps.today: A standing rule forbids any development session from connecting to, probing or touching your running app, because a 'harmless' look in May crashed it mid-session. Sessions may only read log files from outside.
steps.problem: Your request means a session watching the real app as you use it. That cannot be built without changing the rule, so the rule's change is your call before anything else.
steps.proposal: Allow watching only — never controlling — and only while you have a monitor switch on in Settings. Yes changes the rule that way; No means the monitor is limited to what the app writes to its log files.

steps.headline: How should a fixing session see what your running app is doing?
steps.today: The app writes a log file and notes when its window freezes and for how long, but only in that log. Performance testing today is done on a separate copy of the app driven from outside, never on yours.
steps.problem: Freezes and errors that only happen in your real day-to-day use can't be reproduced on the test copy, and the log records too little to diagnose them.
steps.proposal: Three shapes, from safest to most powerful.

options.label: Recorder file
options.summary: While switched on, the app writes freezes, errors, slow moments and memory use to a file. A fixing session reads that file — live, as it grows. Nothing connects to the app.
pros: Nothing ever connects to your app, so it can't crash it the way the May probe did.
Works whether or not a session is watching; the evidence is waiting afterwards.
Fits the safety rule with the smallest change.
cons: A session can only see what the recorder was built to write, not ask new questions on the spot.
A small cost to the app's speed while it's on.

options.label: On-screen panel
options.summary: A small panel inside the app shows freezes, errors and speed as they happen, with a button to copy a report into a fixing session.
pros: You see problems yourself without any session involved.
cons: The panel itself takes screen space and some speed.
A fixing session only learns what you copy across.

options.label: Live connection
options.summary: A fixing session connects directly into the running app and can look at anything inside it.
pros: The most a session can learn; it can investigate on the spot.
cons: Exactly the kind of connection that crashed your app in May.
Opens a door into the app that has to be locked down carefully.
The hardest to build safely.

steps.headline: What should the monitor record?
steps.today: Only window freezes and crashes are noted, and only in the app's general log.
steps.problem: Each extra thing recorded costs a little speed and makes the record longer, so only what you'd actually use should go in.

options.label: Freezes and stutters
options.summary: Every moment the screen stopped responding, how long, and what it was busy doing.
pros: The single most useful thing for 'the app froze'.
cons: Small speed cost while on.

options.label: Errors
options.summary: Every error the app hit behind the scenes, including ones it recovered from silently.
pros: Catches problems you never saw an error message for.
cons: Can be noisy: some errors are harmless.

options.label: Stuck sessions
options.summary: A tool call or model reply that has been waiting far longer than usual.
pros: Spots a hung session even when the screen looks fine.
cons: 'Longer than usual' needs tuning, so early versions may cry wolf.

options.label: Memory and processor use
options.summary: How much memory and processor the app uses over time.
pros: Shows slow leaks that make the app sluggish after hours.
cons: Mostly useful over long stretches, not single moments.

options.label: Typing and scrolling lag
options.summary: How long the screen takes to show a keypress or a scroll.
pros: Measures the lag you feel, as a number.
cons: The costliest to record of the five.

steps.path: The status bar at the bottom of the app
steps.headline: While the monitor is on, should the app show a small sign that it is recording?
steps.today: Nothing would tell you the monitor is running once you leave Settings.
steps.problem: A monitor forgotten for weeks quietly costs speed and grows a large file, and you'd have no reason to suspect it.
steps.proposal: A small 'Recording' dot in the status bar while it's on; clicking it opens the switch. Yes adds it; No leaves the status bar alone.
